Sept jeunes, un message : jamais trop ta: Seven Young People, One Message: It's Never Too Late
Encadrés par la mentor Meryem Saci, sept: Mentored by Meryem Saci, seven young artists took part in the MC Converse 2025 project. The result: the rap song “Jamais Trop Tard.”
Les participants MC Converse 2025, encad: The MC Converse 2025 participants, mentored by Birdzontrack and Meryem Saci, in the Toosik studio with Alex Papineau. Photo credit: Ismaël Koné
Cette année, j’ai eu le privilège de sui: This year, I had the privilege of closely following the third MC Converse project and telling the story of the artists who took part. Seven young people, all different, but united by the same desire: to create a track that looks like them.
Mon rôle ne s’est pas limité à celui de: My role wasn't limited to that of a journalist. I was there at every stage: from the first meetings to the recording, including the writing workshops with Meryem Saci, this edition's mentor. I watched the track Jamais trop tard being created live at the Toosik studio, then the shooting of the video a few days later.
Je me suis sentie tellement bien accueil: I felt so welcome from the very start. The group's energy was beautiful, fluid and natural. There was respect, laughter, debate, mutual support. And above all, a real desire to get a message across together.
Mon principal défi a été de rendre justi: My main challenge was to do justice to each artist, without over-interpreting, without embellishing. Just to convey what they entrusted to me, in their words, with their emotions and sometimes even their silences. “Jamais trop tard” echoes what many young people are living through today. I'm truly proud of every one of them.
Merci à toutes les personnes qui ont ren: Thank you to everyone who made this project possible. And above all, thank you to the artists for their trust.
Ils ne viennent pas du même quartier, n’: They don't come from the same neighbourhood, they aren't the same age, and they don't share the same references. Some of them already knew each other, others not at all. But for two months, they took the time to talk, to write, to advise one another, to laugh too, and above all to record a “banger” together. In La Converse's studios, a real connection formed between Kester, Imene, Akashi Tonny, Kitana, Amine, Bougelite and Drippy. Together, they gave birth to a song: Jamais trop tard.
Alex Papineau (assis), Meryem Saci (debo: Alex Papineau (seated), Meryem Saci (standing at left), Kitana (at right), at the Toosik studio. Photo credit: Ismaël Koné
Encadrés par la mentor <l1>Meryem Saci</: Mentored by <l1>Meryem Saci</l1>, the seven young artists took part in the MC Converse 2025 project. They each recorded a verse or a chorus, carried by their words, their life experiences and their reflections, over an original production by <l2>Birdzonthetrack</l2>. The track was recorded this past May 21 at <l3>Toosik studio</l3> in Ahuntsic. The music video was shot a week later, on May 28, under the Montréal sun.
Ce rap journalistique nous raconte ce qu: This journalistic rap tells us what young people are living through and carries a message of hope.
Pensé comme un projet d’expression citoy: Conceived as a project of civic expression through rap, Jamais trop tard gives a voice to seven young artists who describe what they live, what they feel and what they see around them. Each with their own pen, their own experience, their own perspective.
Le titre, <em>Jamais trop tard</em>, ref: The title, Jamais trop tard, reflects the message they want to share together: it's never too late to get out, to change, to get back up, to find your path, despite the obstacles, the mistakes and the doubts.
Ils ne racontent pas tous les choses de: They don't all tell things the same way, but all of their words come from somewhere: from lived experience, from anger, from the desire to succeed, or simply from a need for truth. Behind every verse, there is a person, a story and a life path.
Voici les artistes derrière le morceau <: Here are the artists behind the track Jamais trop tard.
<l1>Drippy</l1>, 18 ans, c’est une voix:
<l1>Drippy</l1>, 18, is a voice born between two continents and a heart anchored in Montréal.
From Romania to Mexico to the streets of Ahuntsic-Cartierville, he grew up among languages, cultures and sounds. His father was a DJ, and that's probably where his connection to music comes from. Music has been with him since childhood. It helps him speak when words get stuck, to express what he keeps to himself.
Il a commencé à 12 ans, malgré les moque: He started at 12, despite the mockery, despite the doubts. From an old phone to his first late-night recordings in his bedroom, he moved forward on his own, driven by the urge to say what others keep quiet. Today, he keeps going. Not to impress, but to share.
Dans ses textes, il parle d’amour, de ru: In his lyrics, he talks about love, breakups, memories, but also about the stories of the people close to him. He puts himself in other people's shoes, tells of their silences, their pain, their desires.
Il mêle rap, afro beat, reggaeton, franç: He blends rap, Afrobeat, reggaeton, French, Spanish. Everything he is – his roots, his influences, his languages – can be found in his sound. His influences are many: from XXXTentacion to Vacra, by way of Kaza, Zola and the Montréal scene he actively listens to.
« Chaque fois que j’ai un petit peu d’ar: “Every time I have a little bit of money: studio. Straight away. Even if it puts me in debt, I don't care,” he says with determination.
Et d’ailleurs, dans le couplet qu’il a p: And in fact, in the verse he laid down for MC Converse, he talks about an artist who, for lack of means, takes the wrong path to pay for his music-related expenses.
Ses ambitions ? “Je rêve de grandes scèn: His ambitions? “I dream of big stages: Club Soda, the Francos”
Et ce qui le pousse à continuer malgré t: And what keeps him going despite everything:
“Chaque message que je reçois, chaque pe: “Every message I get, every person who recognizes themselves in my lyrics, reminds me that I was right not to give up.”
Kester Milhomme, alias Le petit Kester. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
Kester Milhomme, alias <em><l1>Le petit: Kester Milhomme, alias Le petit Kester, is 19. Born in Montréal, of Haitian and Brazilian descent “for the little exotic touch,” he says, laughing, he grew up in Rivière-des-Prairies – BGP, for the real ones.
Avant même de se mettre à rapper, il fil:
Even before he started rapping, he was already filming comedy videos and posting them online.
A content creator at heart, he began writing his first rap lyrics at 13, to make his friends laugh and to tease them. “My songs are often to make fun of my boys. I've written a lot of diss tracks.”
Son humour, il le cultive en s’inspirant: He cultivates his humour by drawing on Mister V, his absolute idol: “If I have a kid, I'll name him Yvick.”
Mais derrière les rires, il y a aussi de: But behind the laughter, there are also realities he doesn't forget.
Dans son couplet pour MC Converse, il ab: In his verse for MC Converse, he addresses one of the hardest moments he went through with his family: he remembers leaving their public housing apartment (HLM) in RDP to move into a house in Saint-Léonard thanks to his mother's hard work. But barely a year later, his mother lost her job overnight. His family was forced to go back to the same apartment in the same public housing complex.
Ce retour forcé, Kester ne le considère: Kester doesn't see that forced return as a defeat.
« Je veux transmettre la rage de vaincre: “I want to pass on the drive to win again. We fall, but we get back up,” he says. Today, he channels that energy into a style all his own: a mix of spontaneous, funny rap. He also explores R&B, plays with sounds, and claims his taste for “vibey” sounds. “I was born into rap. My dad listened to it all the time,” he explains. Asked how he would describe himself, he answers without hesitation: “Young, funny and engaged content creator.”
Son quartier, Rivière-des-Prairies, rest: His neighbourhood, Rivière-des-Prairies, remains at the heart of his journey. “No matter what I do, I'll always represent RDP,” he declares.
Adam Boughelit, plus connu sous le nom d: Adam Boughelit, better known as Bougelite. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
<l1>Bougelite</l1>, c’est un nom d’artis: <l1>Bougelite</l1> is a stage name born of a classroom misunderstanding: a teacher mispronounced his last name, “Boughelit.” It stuck and became his signature. “There's ‘élite’ in it, I thought that was stylish,” he tells me with a smile. At 17, the young artist from Saint-Michel is studying marketing and management, a strategic choice: he lives music out of passion, but he's also thinking about what comes next, he explains.
Il commence à écrire à 15 ans, lors d’un: He started writing at 15, during a workshop with Mamie Remix, where he turned seniors' words into rap songs. Since then, he has performed on several stages: MC Challenge, Festival jeunesse de Saint-Michel, La Zone.
Auteur, compositeur, interprète, Bougeli: Songwriter, composer, performer, Bougelite does everything himself. He builds his own instrumentals, lays his lyrics over them, works through his ideas solo. Very “low-key” in life, he becomes “arrogant and unapologetic” on stage. “The stage helps me open up. I'm not the same person when I'm up there.”
Dans ses morceaux, il se questionne sur: In his songs, he questions his life choices – school, music, the future – and the impact they have on his daily life. He explores his personal thoughts and isn't afraid to provoke at times, with lines that ask to be interpreted.
“It's okay if they don't understand. I'm going to keep going. And even exaggerate more.”
Et dans le couplet qu’il a posé pour MC: And in the verse he laid down for MC Converse, he hits hard. He compares two realities that young people live today: the street and school. On one side, a young person looking to make money fast, to get their freedom at all costs. On the other, a young person who studies in the hope of one day having a good job and a stable future.
Deux chemins, deux pressions, deux tempo: Two paths, two pressures, two timelines. But the same question behind it all: how are they going to get their financial freedom?
<l1>Imene</l1>, c’est une voix qui s’élè: <l1>Imene</l1> is a voice that rises when it has to, without ever bending. Imene is an artist who, she says, refuses labels, ready-made expectations, and other people's views of what she should be. Born in Algeria, she arrived in Montréal at 16 and grew up in several neighbourhoods in the city's east end. She sings of love, peace, invisible struggles.
« Je ne me vois pas chanter quelque chos: “I can't see myself singing something that isn't aligned with who I am.” Her relationship to art is sacred. She says so herself: “Music is simply part of my way of living. Art, in general, is part of me.”
Éclectique, elle explore le rap par curi: Eclectic, she explores rap out of curiosity, out of a desire to learn. But singing remains her first language. She likes artists like TIF, “for the sincerity of the lyrics, the sensitivity of the melodies, and the balance between emotion and restraint.” What matters to her isn't the style, but what the lyrics stir up.
« Tout ce qui me touche, je m’en inspire: “Everything that touches me, I draw inspiration from.”
Ce qu’elle cherche avant tout, c’est ce: What she seeks above all is what rings true: sincere words, a voice that's fully inhabited, an emotion that leaves a mark, she explains.
Sur scène elle a chanté avec le groupe N: On stage, she has sung with the group Numidz at Nuits d'Afrique, then at the Orchestre symphonique de Montréal's Virée classique, alongside the group Mezghana. Moments when her voice, carried by collective projects, found its place.
Dans la chanson collective de MC Convers: In the MC Converse collective song, her voice carries the chorus.
Une tâche assez difficile, selon elle, q:
A rather difficult task, in her view, which she approached with rigour. She explains that she wanted to sum up in a few words everything the others say in their verses: their journeys, their pain, their hopes. Imene confides that this project means a great deal to her and that she wanted to put all her sensitivity into it, to give rise to a message that speaks to everyone.
“It's a message of hope, for everyone who doubts, who falls, who is still searching for their way, especially young people.”
Ce qu’elle cherche ? “Aller au bout de c:
What is she after? “To go all the way with what makes me happy.”
And what does she hope for? That those who discover her will remember this: “To exist according to your own beliefs. Even when it's hard. Even when it bothers people. Just believe in it.”
AMINE, alias ZVCS. Crédit photo: Édouard: AMINE, alias ZVCS. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
<l1>Amine</l1>, alias ZVCS, a seulement: <l1>Amine</l1>, alias ZVCS, is only 16. Born in Casablanca, he grew up between Morocco and Montréal, from Côte-des-Neiges to Saint-Michel, then Laval.
Il n’aimait ni le rap ni la scène. Jusqu: He liked neither rap nor the stage. Until the day one of his cousins, in Morocco, missed a chance to perform. “I saw that he was full of rage. I promised myself I'd go far in music, for him.” Since then, that promise has carried him. He started freestyling in high school, in the schoolyard, at lunchtime. First studio, first track, first feedback: he realized he had something to say. Today, he writes, raps, produces.
Ses textes parlent des droits humains, d:
His lyrics talk about human rights, injustice, violence, loss.
He draws on his observations as much as his own experience. “What I write is what I live or what I see. I try to make people think.” Among his influences: Lost, Fouki, Manu Militari, but also Zamdane, Diam's, Damso. ZVCS isn't trying to be seen. He simply wants to get across what matters to him.
« Si je pouvais rester dans l’ombre et j: “If I could stay in the shadows and just make music with my voice, I would.”
Dans son couplet pour MC Converse, il fa: In his verse for MC Converse, he goes a step further. He talks about what he saw growing up, as a child and a teenager: poverty, drugs, prostitution. Harsh realities, which he doesn't like to name. But which he chose to put into words, once and for all, to say where he comes from. To explain why he started, why he took certain paths, and why he writes today.
<l1>Kitana</l1>, 19 ans, c’est une voix: <l1>Kitana</l1>, 19, is a voice that hits like a truth you no longer want to hide.
D’origine algérienne, venue de l’est de: Of Algerian origin, from Montréal's east end, she claims a tempered character – with the “plain-spokenness of a girl who never looks down.” She arrived in Montréal at three, grew up here, soaked it in, was shaped by it. Since her teens, music has been part of her life.
Enfermée entre quatre murs, elle écrit s: Shut in between four walls, she wrote her first lyrics: “I started writing when I was in the youth centre. I had nothing to do, so I started like that.” It was her way of putting out what she couldn't say otherwise.
Au départ, elle ne voyait pas la musique: At first, she didn't see music as a serious project. “Before, I just made ‘diss tracks’* with my friends. It wasn't deep.” But things change. Today, she writes and raps to talk about what she has lived through, but also so that others recognize themselves in it. “I know people can ‘relate’ to me. There are people who go through the same thing. I write for them too.” Kitana raps mostly in English, sometimes in French. “English lets me say everything. I feel freer.”
Dans sa partie sur le morceau collectif: In her part of the collective MC Converse track, she talks about her time in the youth centre, what she felt back then, the temptation of the street, the longing for freedom. She wants to show that there isn't just “one path.” There are other possible paths, “you just have to make the right choices.” Today, she keeps writing and laying down her voice. And if she makes music, it's also with the idea of “being everywhere”: rap, singing, social media, social projects. “If I ‘make it,’ I want to start organizations, help others. I don't want to shine all by myself.”
Akashi Tonny. Crédit photo: Édouard Desr: Akashi Tonny. Photo credit: Édouard Desroches
<l1>Akashi Tonny</l1> refuse de se défin: <l1>Akashi Tonny</l1> refuses to define himself by his age. “I'm infinite,” he tells us. Born in Cameroon, he grew up in Saint-Michel. A versatile artist, he dances, slams, writes, performs. He is also deeply invested in the visual and fashion world. But it's music that sits at the centre of his life. “Music saved me. At one point, I'd lost the will to live. Since I started making music, I've found the desire to dream again. (...) If I go a week without making music, I get sick. I feel awful.”
C’est à l’adolescence, alors qu’il trave: It was in his teens, in the midst of a deep existential crisis, that he began to write. He speaks of a need to express himself, to turn what he lives and feels into words. He didn't go looking for it; “music came to [him].” His world is marked by introspection, solitude, melancholy, but also by the desire to find some form of light. Akashi describes his practice as poetry, not rap. “My music is very emotional. I need to be in my bubble to create it.”
Dans le cadre du projet MC Converse, il: As part of the MC Converse project, he says he took on a big challenge: writing and performing a text based on fairly precise guidelines. An unusual approach for him, since he works very spontaneously. His verse tackles heavy themes: violence, abuse, dehumanization. “I talk about things we don't talk about enough. Realities that disturb. But that need to be said.”
Solitaire assumé, Akashi reste souvent à: A self-avowed loner, Akashi often stays apart from the group in the studio. He says he needs silence, mental and physical preparation to deliver a performance that lives up to what he feels. And if he had to define himself, it would be with this phrase: “Be Absolute. I am a butterfly.”‍
